title: IPv4 subnetting: a primer
subtitle: From bits to a checked address plan, by hand. Five modules; each one opens when the modules it rests on are mastered.
size_reason: One skill resting on four ideas: five modules cover it, and a longer course would have to pad.
for: A learner who has seen IP addresses and masks in use and has not yet subnetted by hand.

modules.title: Binary and place value
modules.summary: Reading and writing the eight-bit numbers that every later module works in.

objectives.text: State the place value of each of the eight bit positions in an octet.
Convert an 8-bit binary number to decimal.
Convert a decimal number from 0 to 255 to 8-bit binary.

terms.definition: A binary digit: 0 or 1.
A group of eight bits. An octet takes a value from 0 to 255.
The amount a position contributes when it holds a 1. In binary each place value is twice the one to its right.
The leftmost bit, the one with the largest place value.

theory.heading: Eight positions, each worth twice the one to its right

blocks.text: A **bit** is a digit that is either 0 or 1. An **octet** is a group of eight bits. In an octet each position has a fixed **place value**, and each place value is twice the one to its right, because binary is base two.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: The value of an octet is the sum of the place values of the positions that hold a 1.
The largest octet is `11111111`: 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255. The smallest is `00000000`, which is 0. An octet therefore takes one of 256 values, from 0 to 255.

blocks.label: Assumption
blocks.text: Throughout this course a binary number is written with its most significant bit on the left and is padded to eight digits. `101` and `00000101` are the same number; only the second is in the form used for addresses.

theory.heading: Binary to decimal: add the place values under the ones

items: Write the eight place values above the eight bits.
Ignore every place value that sits above a 0.
Add the place values that remain.

blocks.label: Check
blocks.text: A number whose last bit is 1 is odd, because only the last place value, 1, is odd. If the last bit is 1 and your sum is even, an addition has gone wrong.

theory.heading: Decimal to binary: subtract place values from the left

items: Start at 128. If the place value is no larger than what remains, write 1 and subtract it. Otherwise write 0.
Move one position to the right and repeat with what remains.
Stop after the eighth position. What remains must be 0.

blocks.text:
172    128 fits, leaves 44    write 1
        64 does not fit       write 0
        32 fits, leaves 12    write 1
        16 does not fit       write 0
         8 fits, leaves 4     write 1
         4 fits, leaves 0     write 1
         2 does not fit       write 0
         1 does not fit       write 0

172 = 10101100

blocks.label: Common error
blocks.text: Stopping when the remainder reaches 0 and writing fewer than eight digits. The positions still to come are zeros and must be written: 192 is `11000000`, not `11`.
Eight values recur in every later module, because a subnet mask fills an octet with ones from the left. Learn them as a set.

visuals.title: Flip the bits of an octet
visuals.caption: Each button is one bit, labelled with its place value. The decimal value is the sum of the place values of the bits that are set to 1.
prompts: Before you touch anything, read the starting octet as a decimal number. Then check it against the display.
Make 192, then 224, then 240. What changes each time?
Set only the last bit. Then set every bit. These are the smallest odd value and the largest value.

steps.caption: 172 remains. 128 is no larger than 172, so write 1 and subtract: 44 remains.
44 remains. 64 is larger than 44, so write 0. Nothing is subtracted.

0 remains. 2 is larger than 0, so write 0.
0 remains. 1 is larger than 0, so write 0. Eight digits are written and nothing remains: 172 is `10101100`.

visuals.caption: The top row is what remains before each position is tried. The bottom row is the bit written for that position.

Left four bits, `1011`: add the place values under the ones, 128 + 32 + 16.
Right four bits, `0100`: the only 1 sits under 4.

Left four bits, `1110`: add the place values under the ones.

Right four bits, `1011`: 8 + 2 + 1.

32 and 16 are both larger than 9. Write 0 for each.
8 fits in 9. Write 1; 1 remains.
4 and 2 are both larger than 1. Write 0 for each.

Read the eight digits in order.

8 is larger than what remains. Write 0. Then 4 fits and 2 fits, and 1 does not.

solution.text: 128 is larger than 99. Write 0.
64 fits; 35 remains. 32 fits; 3 remains.

quiz.stem: What is the place value of the third bit from the left in an octet?

options.why: 4 is the third place value counted from the right. Positions in an address are read from the left.
From the left the place values run 128, 64, 32. The third is 32.
3 is the position number. A place value is a power of two, and 3 is not one.
8 is 2^3. The exponent for the third position from the left is 5, not 3.

quiz.stem: How many different values can one octet hold?

options.why: 255 is the largest value. Counting the values from 0 to 255 gives one more than that.
128 is the place value of the leftmost bit, not the number of values.
Eight bits give 2^8 patterns, the values 0 to 255.
8 is the number of bits. Each bit doubles the number of patterns.

quiz.stem: What is `11000000` in decimal?

options.why: The ones sit under 128 and 64, and 128 + 64 = 192.
3 is `00000011`. The two ones were read as if they sat at the right-hand end.
Only the first 1 was counted. The second 1 adds 64.
96 is 64 + 32, which is `01100000`. Each bit was valued one place too low.

quiz.stem: What is `00001111` in decimal?

options.why: 240 is `11110000`, the mirror image. The four ones here are at the right-hand end.
4 is the count of ones. The value is the sum of their place values.
16 is `00010000`, one more than this number.
The ones sit under 8, 4, 2 and 1, and 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15.

quiz.stem: What is 224 as an 8-bit binary number?

options.why: That is 240. One 1 too many: 224 is used up after 128, 64 and 32.
128 + 64 + 32 = 224, so the first three bits are 1 and the rest are 0.
That is 7. The three ones belong at the left-hand end, under the largest place values.
That is 192. After 128 and 64, 32 still fits in what remains.

quiz.stem: What is 10 as an 8-bit binary number?

options.why: That is 16. A single 1 was placed under the nearest larger place value.
That is 80. The digits 1010 were written at the left-hand end.
8 + 2 = 10, so the ones sit under 8 and 2, with four leading zeros.
That is 12, which is 8 + 4. After 8, what remains is 2, and 4 does not fit.

items.stem: Which list gives the place values of an octet from left to right?

options.why: These are the right values in right-to-left order. The leftmost bit is the most significant.
These are position numbers counted from the right, not place values.
Each place value is twice the one to its right, ending at 1.
Every value is one place too high. The rightmost place value is 1.

items.stem: What is the place value of the leftmost bit of an octet?

options.why: The leftmost of eight positions is worth 2^7.
256 is 2^8, the number of values an octet can take, not a place value within it.
255 is the value of an octet with every bit set.
8 is the number of bits in the octet.

items.stem: What is `10101000` in decimal?

options.why: 84 is `01010100`. Each bit was valued one place too low.
21 is `00010101`. The place values were applied from the wrong end.
3 is the count of ones, not the sum of their place values.
The ones sit under 128, 32 and 8, and 128 + 32 + 8 = 168.

items.stem: What is `11111100` in decimal?

options.why: 254 is `11111110`. This number has two zeros at the end, not one.
The ones sit under 128, 64, 32, 16, 8 and 4, which add to 252.
63 is `00111111`, this pattern read from the wrong end.
6 is the count of ones, not the sum of their place values.

items.stem: What is 77 as an 8-bit binary number?

options.why: That is 154. The digits were shifted one place to the left.
64 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 77, so the ones sit under 64, 8, 4 and 1.
That is 75. After 64 and 8, what remains is 5, and 4 fits in 5.
That is 85. After 64, what remains is 13, and 16 does not fit.

items.stem: What is 240 as an 8-bit binary number?

options.why: That is 15. The four ones belong under the four largest place values.
That is 224. After 128, 64 and 32, what remains is 16, and 16 fits.
That is 248. After 128, 64, 32 and 16 nothing remains, so the fifth bit is 0.
128 + 64 + 32 + 16 = 240, so the first four bits are 1.

cheatsheet.label: Binary to decimal
cheatsheet.text: Add the place values of the positions that hold a 1.

cheatsheet.label: Decimal to binary
cheatsheet.text: From 128 down: if the place value fits in what remains, write 1 and subtract it; otherwise write 0. Always eight digits.

items: An octet runs from 0 to 255: 256 values.
A last bit of 1 means an odd number.

modules.title: Address structure and prefix length
modules.summary: What the 32 bits of an address are, and how a prefix length cuts them into a network part and a host part.

objectives.text: Describe an IPv4 address as 32 bits written as four decimal octets.
State how a prefix length divides the 32 bits into a network part and a host part.
Convert between a prefix length and a dotted-decimal subnet mask.

terms.definition: A 32-bit number that identifies an interface on a network.
The written form of an address: four octets, each in decimal, joined by dots.
The leading bits of an address, shared by every address on the same network.
The remaining bits, which tell one interface on a network from another.
The number of bits in the network part, written after a slash, as in `/26`.
A 32-bit number with a 1 in every network position and a 0 in every host position.

theory.heading: Thirty-two bits, written as four decimal octets

blocks.text: An **IPv4 address** is a 32-bit number. For people it is written in **dotted decimal**: the 32 bits are cut into 4 octets, each octet is written in decimal, and the four numbers are joined by dots.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: Each of the four numbers is one octet, so each lies from 0 to 255. `192.168.10.300` is not an address, because 300 does not fit in eight bits.

blocks.label: Assumption
blocks.text: This course covers IPv4 only. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long and are written differently.

theory.heading: The prefix length is where the network part ends

blocks.text: Every address has two parts. The **network part** is the leading bits, shared by every address on the same network. The **host part** is the remaining bits, which tell one interface on that network from another.
The **prefix length** is the number of bits in the network part. It is written after a slash: `192.168.10.77/24` has a network part of 24 bits and a host part of 8 bits.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: For a prefix length p, the network part is the first p bits and the host part is the last 32 - p bits.
A street address works the same way. The street name is shared by every house on the street, and the house number tells the houses apart. The prefix length says how much of the address is street.

blocks.label: Common error
blocks.text: Assuming the boundary always falls on a dot. It falls on a dot only for /8, /16 and /24. For /26 it falls inside the fourth octet, and that octet must then be handled in binary.

theory.heading: The subnet mask says the same thing in dotted decimal

blocks.text: A **subnet mask** is a 32-bit number with a 1 in every network position and a 0 in every host position. A prefix length of p gives a mask of p ones followed by 32 - p zeros. The mask and the prefix length carry the same information in two notations.
From a prefix length to a mask:

items: Write 255 for each whole group of eight ones.
Subtract 8 from the prefix length for each whole group. Fill the next octet with that many ones from the left and convert it to decimal.
Write 0 for every octet that remains.

blocks.text: For /20: two whole groups give 255.255, and 4 ones are left over. `11110000` is 240. The last octet is 0. The mask is 255.255.240.0.
From a mask to a prefix length:

items: Count 8 for each octet that is 255.
Convert the octet that is neither 255 nor 0 to binary and count its ones.
Add the counts.

blocks.text: For 255.255.255.224: three octets of 255 give 24, and 224 is `11100000`, which has 3 ones. The prefix length is /27.

blocks.label: Check
blocks.text: A valid mask is ones followed by zeros with no gaps. A mask octet can therefore only be 0, 128, 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254 or 255, and only 0 may follow an octet that is below 255. `255.255.255.100` is not a mask.

visuals.title: Move the boundary between network and host
visuals.caption: Each cell is one bit of an address, in four octets. N cells are the network part and H cells are the host part. An octet of the mask changes only while the boundary is inside that octet.
prompts: Move the prefix length from 24 to 30 one bit at a time. Say each mask aloud before you read it.
Find the three prefix lengths in this range at which the boundary sits exactly on a dot.
At /20, which octet of the mask is neither 255 nor 0?

visuals.title: One address under two prefix lengths

states.summary: The boundary sits on the third dot.
The boundary sits two bits inside the fourth octet.

visuals.caption: The address is the same 32 bits in both. Only the prefix length differs, and with it the answer to which bits name the network. An address without a prefix length does not say which network it is on.

worked.title: Between a prefix length and a mask

steps.text: Count the whole groups of eight ones in 19.
Write 255 for each whole group.
Find the ones left over.
Fill the third octet with 3 ones from the left and convert it.
Write 0 for the octet that remains.
Count the whole groups of eight ones in 29, and write 255 for each.
Find the ones left over.
Fill the fourth octet with that many ones from the left and convert it to decimal.
Write the whole mask.

blank.label: Subnet mask
blank.hint: Three octets of 255, then your fourth octet.

independent.problem: A device shows the mask 255.255.252.0. Give the prefix length and the number of host bits.

solution.text: Count 8 for each octet that is 255.
Convert 252 to binary and count its ones.
Add the counts.
Subtract from 32 for the host bits.

quiz.stem: How many bits are in an IPv4 address?

options.why: 4 is the number of octets. Each octet is eight bits.
8 is the number of bits in one octet. There are four octets.
Four octets of eight bits each.
12 is the largest number of decimal digits an address can show. Digits are not bits.

quiz.stem: Which of these is **not** a valid IPv4 address?

options.why: Valid. Zero is a legal value for any octet.
Valid. 255 is the largest value an octet can hold, and it fits.
Valid. Every octet lies from 0 to 255.
256 does not fit in eight bits. The largest octet is 255.

quiz.stem: In 172.16.5.9/20, how many bits form the host part?

options.why: The host part is the last 32 - 20 bits.
20 is the length of the network part. The host part is what is left of the 32 bits.
4 is how far the boundary reaches into the third octet. The host part also includes the rest of that octet and all of the fourth.
8 would be right for /24. Here the boundary is inside the third octet, not on the last dot.

quiz.stem: Two addresses agree in their first 24 bits, and the prefix length is /24. What does that establish?

options.why: Their host parts, the last eight bits, may still differ.

options.text: They are on the same network
options.why: The network part is the first 24 bits, and those are identical.
The fourth octet is the host part here. It is what tells the two apart.

options.text: Nothing, until the mask is known
options.why: The prefix length is the mask in another notation. It is already known.

quiz.stem: Which subnet mask is /26?

options.why: That is /27. One bit too many was set in the fourth octet.
That is /25. One bit too few was set in the fourth octet.
The prefix length was written as the last octet. 26 is not a run of ones from the left.
Three octets of 255 use 24 ones. The 2 left over give `11000000`, which is 192.

quiz.stem: Which prefix length is the mask 255.255.240.0?

options.why: 240 would be the fourth octet of /28. Here it is the third octet.
Two octets of 255 give 16, and 240 is `11110000`, which adds 4.
Only one octet of 255 was counted. There are two.
Every non-zero octet was counted as 8. The third octet, 240, holds only 4 ones.

items.stem: What does each of the four numbers in a dotted-decimal address represent?

options.text: One octet: 8 bits of the 32-bit address, written in decimal
options.why: The 32 bits are cut into four groups of 8 and each group is written as a decimal number.

options.text: One level of the network, from largest to smallest
options.why: The dots are for reading. The network boundary is set by the prefix length, not by the dots.

options.text: Three bits each, twelve bits in all
options.why: Up to three decimal digits are needed to write an octet, but an octet is eight bits.

options.text: One decimal number with no fixed range
options.why: Each number is eight bits, so it is limited to 0 to 255.

items.stem: What is the largest value one number in a dotted-decimal address can have?

options.why: 256 is how many values an octet can take, counting 0. The largest of them is one less.
Three decimal digits can be written, but the number must fit in eight bits.
Eight bits all set to 1 add to 255.
128 is the place value of the leftmost bit alone.

items.stem: In 10.20.30.40/22, how many bits are in the network part and how many in the host part?

options.why: The two parts are swapped. The prefix length counts network bits.
That assumes the boundary sits on the last dot. /22 puts it two bits earlier.
The prefix length is the network part, and 32 - 22 bits remain for hosts.
The boundary was moved back to the nearest dot. It sits where the prefix length says.

items.stem: A prefix length is raised from /24 to /26. What happens to the host part?

options.text: It grows by 2 bits, from 8 to 10
options.why: The direction is reversed. A longer prefix takes bits away from the host part.

options.text: It shrinks by 2 bits, from 8 to 6
options.why: The network part gains the two bits that the host part loses.

options.text: It stays at 8 bits; only the mask changes
options.why: The mask and the prefix length are the same statement. Changing one changes the split.
2 is the size of the change, not what is left.

items.stem: What is the subnet mask for /27?

options.why: That is /26. After 24 ones, 3 are left over, not 2.
That is /28. After 24 ones, 3 are left over, not 4.
That is /19. The partly filled octet is the fourth, not the third.
Three octets of 255, then 3 ones from the left: `11100000`, which is 224.

items.stem: What is the prefix length of the mask 255.255.255.248?

options.why: /30 has a fourth octet of 252.
/28 has a fourth octet of 240.
Three octets of 255 give 24, and 248 is `11111000`, which adds 5.
Only the ones in the last octet were counted. The three octets of 255 add 24.

cheatsheet.label: Prefix length
cheatsheet.text: `/p` means the first p bits are the network part and the last 32 - p bits are the host part.

cards.back: The number of leading bits that form the network part.

modules.title: Network and broadcast addresses
modules.summary: Finding the first and last address of the block a host lives in, and the usable range between them.

objectives.text: Find the network address of a host from its address and prefix length.
Find the broadcast address and the first and last usable host addresses of a subnet.
Decide whether two addresses are in the same subnet.

terms.definition: The address in a subnet whose host bits are all 0. It names the subnet and is not given to a host.
The address in a subnet whose host bits are all 1. It is the last address of the block and is not given to a host.
The addresses strictly between the network address and the broadcast address.
The octet in which the mask is neither 255 nor 0: the octet the boundary falls inside.
The number of values one subnet spans in the interesting octet: 256 minus the mask value in that octet.
A bit-by-bit operation whose result is 1 only where both inputs are 1.

theory.heading: The network address: host bits all zero

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: The **network address** of a subnet is the address whose host bits are all zero. It names the subnet itself and is not assigned to a host.
To find it from any address in the subnet, keep the network bits and clear the host bits. Bit by bit, that is the **AND** of the address and the mask: a result bit is 1 only where both inputs are 1.

There is a quicker method that stays in decimal. The **interesting octet** is the one in which the mask is neither 255 nor 0. The **block size** is 256 minus the mask value in that octet. Subnets begin at multiples of the block size, so the network value is the largest multiple of the block size that is not above the address value in that octet.

items: Copy the address octets under a mask octet of 255.
In the interesting octet, find the block size: 256 minus the mask octet.
Take the largest multiple of the block size that is not above the address octet.
Write 0 in every octet under a mask octet of 0.

blocks.text: For 192.168.10.77/26 the mask octet is 192, so the block size is 64. The multiples of 64 are 0, 64, 128 and 192. The largest that is not above 77 is 64. The network address is 192.168.10.64.

blocks.label: Special case
blocks.text: When the prefix length falls on a dot, as it does for /8, /16 and /24, there is no interesting octet. Every host octet of the network address is simply 0.

theory.heading: The broadcast address and the usable range

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: The **broadcast address** of a subnet is the address whose host bits are all one. It is the last address of the block. A packet sent to it is addressed to every host on the subnet, so it is not assigned to a host.
In the interesting octet, the broadcast value is the network value plus the block size, minus one. Any octets to the right of the interesting octet are all host bits, so they are 255.
The **usable host range** is everything strictly between the two: the first usable host is the network address plus one, and the last usable host is the broadcast address minus one.

network      01 000000   64     host bits all 0
first host   01 000001   65
last host    01 111110   126
broadcast    01 111111   127    host bits all 1

When the interesting octet is not the last one, the same steps apply in that octet. For 172.20.70.5/20 the mask is 255.255.240.0, the block size in the third octet is 16, and 70 falls in the block that starts at 64. The network address is 172.20.64.0, the broadcast address is 172.20.79.255, and the usable range is 172.20.64.1 to 172.20.79.254.

blocks.label: Common error
blocks.text: Giving an address ending in .255 as the broadcast address of every subnet. That holds only when the whole last octet is host bits. The broadcast address of 192.168.10.77/26 is 192.168.10.127.

blocks.label: Scope
blocks.text: The rules here apply to prefix lengths up to /30. On a point-to-point link a /31 uses both of its addresses for hosts, and a /32 names a single host. Neither is covered in this course.
blocks.source: RFC 3021, Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point Links (December 2000), read 9 Oct 2026.

blocks.text: Two addresses are in the same subnet exactly when the same prefix length gives them the same network address. Compute the network address of each and compare.
Closeness of the numbers proves nothing. 192.168.10.126 and 192.168.10.129 differ by 3 and, under /26, lie in different subnets.

blocks.label: Why it matters
blocks.text: A host delivers directly to addresses inside its own subnet and sends everything else to its gateway. A host with the wrong prefix length misjudges which is which.

visuals.title: Which block does the address fall in?
visuals.caption: The line is the fourth octet, cut into blocks by the prefix length. The marked band is the block that holds the address. Its left edge is the network value, and the last value before its right edge is the broadcast value.
prompts: Under /26, set the octet to 126 and then to 129. Did the block change?
Under /28, decide which block holds 200 before you move the marker.
Keep the octet at 77 and step through the four prefix lengths. Watch the network value change while the address stays put.

visuals.title: The fourth octet of 192.168.10.77/26, bit by bit

steps.caption: Write the interesting octet of the address, 77, in binary.
Write the mask octet, 192, beneath it. Its 2 ones mark the network bits of this octet; its 6 zeros mark host bits.
AND each column: a 1 survives only where the mask has a 1. The six host bits become 0. The result is `01000000`, which is 64, the network value.
Now keep the two network bits and set the six host bits to 1 instead. The result is `01111111`, which is 127, the broadcast value.

visuals.caption: Network and broadcast differ only in the host bits: all 0 for one, all 1 for the other.

worked.title: Network address, usable range and broadcast address

full.problem: A host has the address 172.16.45.200/27. Find the network address, the broadcast address and the usable range.

steps.text: Write the mask for /27.
The interesting octet is the fourth. Find the block size: 256 minus 224.
Find the largest multiple of 32 that is not above 200. The multiples near 200 are 160, 192 and 224.
For the broadcast value add the block size and subtract one: 192 + 32 - 1.
The usable range lies strictly between the two.

partial.problem: A host has the address 10.4.9.150/28. Find the network address, the broadcast address and the usable range.

steps.text: Write the mask for /28.
The interesting octet is the fourth. Find the block size.
Find the largest multiple of the block size that is not above 150, and write the network address.
Add the block size and subtract one, and write the broadcast address.
The usable range lies strictly between the two.

independent.problem: A host has the address 192.168.3.99/25. Give the network address, the first and last usable hosts, and the broadcast address.

solution.text: The mask for /25 is 255.255.255.128, so the block size in the fourth octet is 256 - 128.
The multiples of 128 are 0 and 128. The largest that is not above 99 is 0.
Add the block size and subtract one: 0 + 128 - 1.

modules.title: Counting hosts and subnets
modules.summary: How many addresses a prefix length holds, how many subnets a longer prefix makes, and how to choose a prefix length for a requirement.

objectives.text: Calculate the number of addresses and of usable hosts for a prefix length.
Calculate how many subnets are made by lengthening a prefix.
Choose the longest prefix length that still holds a required number of hosts or subnets.

terms.definition: The addresses in a subnet that can be given to hosts: every address except the network address and the broadcast address.
Bits moved from the host part to the network part when a prefix is lengthened.
The bits of the host part. For a prefix length p there are 32 - p of them.

blocks.text: With h host bits there are `2^h` bit patterns, so a subnet holds `2^h` addresses. Two of them are not given to hosts: the pattern of all zeros is the network address and the pattern of all ones is the broadcast address.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: For a prefix length p: host bits `h = 32 - p`. Addresses `= 2^h`. Usable hosts `= 2^h - 2`.

blocks.label: Assumption
blocks.text: Subtracting two applies to prefix lengths up to /30. The prefix lengths /31 and /32 are special cases outside this course.

blocks.label: Common error
blocks.text: Leaving out the subtraction when a question asks for hosts, or applying it when a question asks for addresses. Read which of the two is asked for.
Lengthening a prefix moves bits from the host part to the network part. These are **borrowed bits**. With s borrowed bits the original network is cut into `2^s` subnets of equal size.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: From /p to /q, with q greater than p: borrowed bits `s = q - p`, and the number of subnets is `2^s`.

A /24 lengthened to /27 borrows 3 bits and makes 8 subnets. Each has 5 host bits: 32 addresses and 30 usable hosts. Nothing is created or lost: 8 subnets of 32 addresses are the 256 addresses of the /24.

blocks.label: The trade
blocks.text: Every borrowed bit doubles the number of subnets and halves the number of addresses in each.

theory.heading: Choosing a prefix length for a requirement

blocks.text: Requirements arrive as counts: so many hosts in a subnet, or so many subnets. Turn each count into a number of bits.
For a number of hosts:

items: Add 2 to the number of hosts, for the network address and the broadcast address.
Find the smallest power of two that is at least that sum. Its exponent is the number of host bits h.
The prefix length is 32 - h.

blocks.text: For 50 hosts: 50 + 2 = 52. The smallest power of two that is at least 52 is 64, which is `2^6`. Six host bits give a prefix length of /26, which has 62 usable hosts.
For a number of subnets:

items: Find the smallest power of two that is at least the number of subnets. Its exponent is the number of bits to borrow.
Add that number to the original prefix length.

blocks.text: For 5 subnets of a /24: the smallest power of two that is at least 5 is 8, which is `2^3`. Borrow 3 bits: the new prefix length is /27.

blocks.label: Boundary case
blocks.text: 62 hosts fit a /26 with nothing to spare. 63 hosts do not: 63 + 2 = 65, which is more than 64, so 63 hosts need a /25.

blocks.label: Check
blocks.text: A plan often has both requirements at once. After choosing a prefix length for the number of subnets, compute the usable hosts it leaves and compare that with the host requirement.

modules.title: Splitting a network
modules.summary: Putting the two skills together: cut a network into equal subnets, list each one, and check the plan against its requirements.

objectives.text: Divide a network into equal subnets and list each subnet's network address.
Give the usable range and the broadcast address of any subnet in a plan.
Design a plan that meets stated subnet and host requirements, and check it against them.

terms.definition: A list of the subnets a network is divided into, each with its network address, usable range and broadcast address.
Subnets that all have the same prefix length, and so the same size.

theory.heading: List the subnets by stepping the block size

blocks.text: Dividing a network into equal subnets uses three decisions you have already met. Choose the new prefix length (Module 4). Find the block size in the interesting octet (Module 3). Then list the network addresses: start at the original network address and add the block size until the original block is used up.

items: Choose the new prefix length from the requirement.
Find the block size: 256 minus the new mask's value in the interesting octet.
The first subnet starts at the original network address.
Each further subnet starts one block size later. Stop when the number of subnets, 2 to the power of the borrowed bits, is reached.

blocks.text: Take 192.168.50.0/24 cut into /26 subnets. 2 bits are borrowed, so there are 4 subnets. The mask octet is 192 and the block size is 64. The subnets start at 0, 64, 128 and 192 in the fourth octet.

blocks.label: Check
blocks.text: The last subnet must end exactly where the original network ends. Here the fourth subnet ends at 192.168.50.255, which is also the broadcast address of the original /24.

blocks.label: Scope
blocks.text: The first subnet, which begins at the original network address, is counted and used like any other. Older texts set aside the first and last subnets; that practice is obsolete.
blocks.source: RFC 1878, Variable Length Subnet Table For IPv4 (December 1995), read 9 Oct 2026.

blocks.text: For each subnet, the broadcast address is one below the next subnet's network address, and the usable range lies strictly between the network address and the broadcast address. Fill the plan row by row. Each row must meet the next with no gap and no overlap, and that exposes slips in arithmetic.

blocks.label: Common error
blocks.text: Leaving a gap between subnets, or giving one address two roles. Adjacent subnets touch: the broadcast address 192.168.50.63 is followed at once by the network address 192.168.50.64.

theory.heading: Design to a requirement, then check it

blocks.text: A requirement usually fixes two things at once: how many subnets, and how many hosts in the largest of them. A plan is correct only if the chosen prefix length satisfies both.

items: From the number of subnets, find the bits to borrow (Module 4).
From the prefix length that results, compute the usable hosts in each subnet.
Compare that with the largest host requirement. If it does not fit, equal subnets of this network cannot meet the requirement, and the correct answer is to say so.
If it fits, list the subnets and complete each row.

blocks.text: Requirement: from 192.168.50.0/24, four departments of at most 50 hosts each. Four subnets need 2 borrowed bits, so the prefix length is /26. A /26 has 62 usable hosts, and 62 is at least 50. The plan above meets the requirement, with 12 addresses to spare in each subnet.

blocks.label: When it cannot be done
blocks.text: From a /24, five departments of 50 hosts each cannot be met with equal subnets. Five subnets need 3 borrowed bits, which gives /27, and a /27 holds only 30 hosts. Say that, and say what would fix it: a larger network, or subnets of unequal size.

blocks.label: Scope
blocks.text: Subnets of unequal size use the same rules, applied to the largest subnet first. This primer stops at equal subnets.

The subnet number was written as the octet. Subnets start at multiples of the block size.

items.stem: 172.16.5.0/24 is cut into 8 equal subnets. What are the new prefix length and the step between network addresses?

options.why: The prefix length is right. The step is the block size, 256 minus the mask octet, not the prefix length.
A /26 borrows 2 bits and makes only 4 subnets.
The number of subnets was added to the prefix length. Add the number of borrowed bits.
Eight subnets need 3 borrowed bits. The mask octet for /27 is 224, so the block size is 32.

items.stem: In a /28 plan for 192.168.1.0/24, what is the broadcast address of the subnet 192.168.1.48/28?

options.why: That is the network address of the next subnet. The broadcast address is one below it.
That is the last usable host of the subnet.
The block size is 16, so the block runs from 48 to 63. The last address is the broadcast address.
That is the broadcast address of the undivided /24.

items.stem: In a /27 plan for 10.1.1.0/24, what is the first usable host of the fifth subnet?

options.why: The block size is 32. The fifth subnet starts at 128, and its first usable host is one above that.
That is the network address of the fifth subnet, which is not given to a host.
That is the first host of the sixth subnet. The first subnet starts at 0, not at 32.
The subnet number was written as the octet.

items.stem: From 192.168.0.0/24, a plan needs 3 subnets of at least 60 hosts each. Which choice meets both requirements?

options.why: There are enough subnets, but 30 hosts is below the 60 required.
There are enough hosts, but 2 subnets is below the 3 required.
Three subnets need 2 borrowed bits. What remains holds 62 hosts, which covers 60.
It can. 60 + 2 = 62, which fits in the 64 addresses of a /26, and a /24 holds four of those.

items.stem: From 10.0.0.0/24, a plan needs 9 subnets of at least 20 hosts each. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: Use /27: 30 hosts is enough, and 8 subnets is close to 9
options.why: A requirement is met or it is not. Eight subnets do not provide nine.

options.text: Use /28: its 16 subnets cover the 9 needed
options.why: The subnets are enough, but the host requirement was not checked. Each holds fewer than 20.

options.text: Equal subnets cannot do it: 9 subnets need /28, which holds 14 hosts
options.why: Nine subnets force 4 borrowed bits, and the 4 host bits that remain hold fewer hosts than required.

options.text: Use /29: more subnets leave more room for hosts
options.why: The reverse. Every borrowed bit halves the addresses in each subnet. A /29 holds 6 hosts.

cards.back: Start at the original network address and add the block size each time.

cards.back: One below it.

cards.back: Enough subnets, and enough usable hosts in the largest one.

cards.front: A /24 into 5 equal subnets of 50 hosts: possible?
cards.back: No. Five subnets need /27, which holds 30 hosts.

cards.back: Two addresses in every subnet: its network address and its broadcast address.

cards.front: How do you know a list of subnets is complete?
cards.back: The last subnet's broadcast address equals the original network's broadcast address.
